## What you should be able to do tonight

- State the five cost components and the source of each, from memory.
- Give the net Sharpe relationship and evaluate it for a strategy with 400 percent annual turnover.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>35 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Finish anything outstanding from days 148 to 153. The per-fill cost recording is the piece to have working, because week 23's tests assert against it.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [15 min]{.task-min} Closed book: the five components, the impact exponent and what it implies for capacity, the net Sharpe relationship, and the three costs that are assumed rather than measured. Then check.

## Drill <span class='task-total'>interview thread</span>

Spaced repetition, not cramming. Every drill in the year is collected on the [drills page](../drills.qmd).

::: {.task-list .drill}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> Arithmetic, timed, twenty-second sitting. Ten two-digit multiplications, the sevenths, and 250 divided by 7, 400 divided by 13 and 1000 divided by 17 to one decimal.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> Optional stopping applied to a game: you draw cards one at a time from a shuffled deck and may stop at any point, winning if the next card is red. What is the best strategy and its value? The answer is surprising and the argument is a martingale one.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> Expected value under a budget: you may pay to roll a die up to three times, keeping the last roll. What is the game worth, and what are the two thresholds in the optimal policy? State both numbers.
:::
:::
